title: DECLARE CURSOR fails with Amazon Redshift
description:
As far as I can tell, this problem is unique to using RPostgres with Amazon Redshift. (I.e. creating a cursor on a 'pure' PostgreSQL system seems to work.)

Redshift is known to have compatibility quirks, **but** this does work when using RPostgreSQL as the DBI driver, so it appears to be something unique to the way RPostgres is interpreting Redshift's returned result.
(Other transaction commands/queries/etc. work with RPostgres, I've only encountered this problem with cursor declaration so far.)
```R
library(DBI)                                                                                                      
conn <- dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), host = <redacted>, port = <redacted>, dbname = <redacted>, user = <redacted>)
dbBegin(conn)                                                                                                     
dbExecute(conn, "DECLARE foo CURSOR FOR SELECT 1")                                                                
#> Error in result_create(conn@ptr, statement): Failed to prepare query: ERROR:  Query cancelled on user's request
```
Here's the same sequence with RPostgreSQL:
```R
library(DBI)                                                                                                          
conn <- dbConnect(RPostgreSQL::PostgreSQL(), host = <redacted>, port = <redacted>, dbname = <redacted>, user = <redacted>)
dbBegin(conn)                                                                                                         
#> [1] TRUE
dbExecute(conn, "DECLARE foo CURSOR FOR SELECT 1")                                                                    
#> [1] 0
```
DBI/driver info:
```R
packageVersion("DBI")        
#> [1] '0.7.13'
packageVersion("RPostgres")  
#> [1] '0.1.12'
packageVersion("RPostgreSQL")
#> [1] '0.6.2'
```
I've seen this problem using both Linux and Mac clients, with these libpq versions:
 * (Amazon) Linux: libpq 9.5.8-1
 * Mac OS 10.11: libpq 9.6.5

I'm not terribly familiar with libpq, but I can take a stab at capturing the output from a PQexec call where a cursor is declared. Alternatively, I can also set up a minimal AWS Redshift cluster for you to use if you'd like to have a source against which to try testing. (If the latter, then we'll have to privately arrange for me to give you login credentials or get an [AWS IAM ARN](http://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/aws-arns-and-namespaces.html#arn-syntax-iam) from you.)

title: Support special types
description:
The current way to support new types seems to [hard code the `typelem` in PqResult.h](https://github.com/r-dbi/RPostgres/blob/master/src/PqResult.h#L261). For types from extensions (such as Postgis), it seems the `typelem` returned can be quite variable (see https://github.com/r-dbi/RPostgres/issues/114 as an example). I believe the `typelem` is not a garantee of the `typname` in PostgreSQL; they are maintained in `pg_types` table (`select * from pg_type;`).

My understanding is that to support special types and facilitate extending RPostgres, it would require to have a generic type conversion function that could return the `typelem` along with R type. I'm brainstorming here, but maybe passing something like e.g. `structure(c("A", "B"), class=c("18", "character"))`, where "18" is PostgreSQL `typelem` of `CHAR`, to a generic `finalize_type()` could work. Even kinder would be to lookup the `typname` (and cache it) rather than provide the `typelem`.

The `Unknown field type` warning would only be thrown by the generic `finalize_type`. But the important part is that I couldn't find a way to access the `typelem` from outside, and I believe it is required to support special types.

title: Request to add PostGIS support
description:
I'm following up on a [tweet exchange](https://twitter.com/hadleywickham/status/723280840352886784) with Hadley. It would be spectacular RPostgres offered PostGIS support (support for PostgreSQL tables that have a geom).

I can't give a perfectly reproducible example since it will depend on your versions of PostGIS etc, but here is an attempt
### Create a spatial DB from the command line

``` batch
createdb --host localhost --port 5433 --username postgres --template postgis_21_sample  mypostgis 
```
### Create a new table, add a geometry column and fill with one polygon (use psql or pgAdmin)

``` sql
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS buildings;
CREATE TABLE buildings ( ID int4, name varchar(25) );
SELECT AddGeometryColumn('public', 'buildings', 'geom', 4326, 'MULTIPOLYGON', 2);
INSERT INTO buildings VALUES(1, 'some name', ST_GeomFromText('MULTIPOLYGON(((-76.5088 42.454, -76.4577 42.45921,  -76.448 42.415889, 
-76.5157 42.4199, -76.5088 42.454)))', 4326));
CREATE INDEX bldg_gist ON buildings USING gist(geom);
```
### In R show what happens with `RPostgres`

You can read in the non-spatial fields just fine, but you get a warning and you get the raw geom data when your query includes the spatial variable (geom). Ideally, if you query against a spatial file it would return some kind of `sp` object like, in this case, a `SpatialPolygonsDataFrame`.

``` r
library(RPostgres)
con <- dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(),dbname = 'mypostgis', 
                 host = 'localhost', 
                 port = 5433,
                 user = 'postgres',
                 password = 'xxx')

res <- dbSendQuery(con, "SELECT id, name FROM buildings")
dbFetch(res)
#   id      name
#1  1 some name

res <- dbSendQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM buildings")
# Warning: Unknown field type (16400) in column geom
dat <- dbFetch(res)
dat
#   id      name
#1  1 some name
#                                                                                                                                                                                                                   geom
#1 0106000020E610000001000000010300000001000000050000001B0DE02D902053C0
# 273108AC1C3A454045D8F0F44A1D53C082FFAD64C73A4540E9263108AC1C53C011E2CAD93B
# 35454005A3923A012153C092CB7F48BF3545401B0DE02D902053C0273108AC1C3A4540
class(dat)
# data.frame
```
### The `postGIStools` package offers some support

With the postGIStools package you can read in PostGIS data

``` r
con <- dbConnect(RPostgreSQL::PostgreSQL(),dbname = 'mypostgis', 
                 host = 'localhost', 
                 port = 5433,
                 user = 'postgres',
                 password = 'spatial')
library(postGIStools)

# SELECT * FROM buildings does not work for some reason
dat <- get_postgis_query(con, "SELECT id, name, geom FROM buildings", 
                         geom_name = "geom")
class(dat)
# [1] "SpatialPolygonsDataFrame"
# attr(,"package")
# [1] "sp"
```

This is perfect except I found it to be slow on a medium size table. With 400k points, it took a pretty long time.
### Speed

The image below shows that it takes almost 5 minutes to read in 400k points as a spatial file, but it can be read in faster if I write to shapefile first and then use `readOGR`. To me this suggests that there is likely a faster way to read this data directly into R.

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1395177/15044739/9301e49c-12a4-11e6-9cf0-f24c10f84898.png)
### Additional discussion on this

I'm not sure what the speediest way to bring in spatial data from PostGIS but I think bringing in a table of just 400k points should take less than 5 minutes as it seems to with postGIStools. And, given the example above where I write to shapefile and read in in half the time, it's clear that there should be better alternatives. There is some discussion about this at the [postGIStools GitHub site](https://github.com/SESYNC-ci/postGIStools/issues/3).

title: PQprepare vs PQexec
description:
This is less a specific issue and more a high-level question about RPostgres' architecture. The use of PQprepare (and PQgetResult) for all calls prevents multiple statements from being executed in a single call, which PQexec supports (while returning PGresult of the final statement). One common use case for this would be streaming contents of an SQL file to a DBI connection, like so:
```R
readr::read_file("my_file") %>% DBI::dbExecute(dbconn, .)  ## or dbGetQuery
```
Is there any planned path with RPostgres to allow use of PQexec? (Perhaps via a configurable option?)
PQexec is already used when copying-in data, but all other code paths seem to opt for the PQprepare/PQgetResult paradigm, which for dbExecute and dbGetQuery seem to result in additional overhead & restrictions.

title: should dbRollback warn (vs error) when not within a transaction block?
description:
In most SQL applications, ROLLBACK is idempotent. When not in a transaction block some SQL back-ends warn, but PostgreSQL specifically does _not_ error. Here's an example psql session:
```
dbname=> BEGIN;
BEGIN
dbname=> SELECT 1;
 ?column?
----------
        1
(1 row)

dbname=> ROLLBACK;
ROLLBACK
dbname=> ROLLBACK;
WARNING:  there is no transaction in progress
ROLLBACK
```
[This line](https://github.com/r-dbi/RPostgres/blob/d1a4c8063aec20149e1e147bad8d1d58c0d89af4/R/transactions.R#L58) throws an error if not within a transaction, which is unexpected for users familiar with PostgreSQL. Should that be a warning instead?

title: Redshift integer in integer64 format
description:
The Redshift output of my `count(...)` will always be returned as `integer64`, even if the integer is just in the 100 - 1000 range. This creates some problems, e.g.,

- `scales::comma(x)` will return the number as a string without comma.
- The integer get parsed into something like 1.482197e-323 during `print`/`cat`.

I reverted the version to [v0.1-8](https://github.com/r-dbi/RPostgres/releases/tag/v0.1-8), and everything worked fine. Something in [v0.1-9](https://github.com/r-dbi/RPostgres/releases/tag/v0.1-9) could have caused this behavior.

As suggested in this [SO post](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45171762/set-dbgetquery-to-return-integer64-as-integer), I casted the output to `int` post query, and it worked. However, in my actual production code, I have 20+ files with 10 ~ 20 count lines from each. I am just wondering if there is a better solution for Redshift instances.

title: Using PostgreSQL functions with dplyr::select
description:
I have a table with a column called `response` which has the data type `json`. PostgreSQL has nice utility functions for manipulating `json`. One of those functions is [json_populate_recordset](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.3/static/functions-json.html) which lets you query a table like this:

| response (json) |
| --- |
| [{"id": 3, "name": "file 1"}, {"id": 5, "name": "file 2"}] | 

in this form:

| id (int) | name (text) |
| --- | --- |
| 3 | file 1 |
| 5 | file 2 |

with a query like this:

```sql
SELECT (json_populate_recordset(null::custom_type, response)).*
FROM "my_table"
```

My approach to generate that query in dplyr was like this:

```r
dplyr::tbl(con, "my_table") %>%
    dplyr::select(json = sql("(json_populate_recordset(null::custom_type, response)).*"))
```

but it fails with:

```r
#> Error: Unknown column `(json_populate_recordset(null::json_type2, response::json->'files')).*` 
```

If it let the use generate this query, there would be no problem:

```sql
SELECT (json_populate_recordset(null::custom_type, response)).* AS "json"
FROM "my_table"
```

I found out that `tidyselect::var_select` has an argument called `.strict` which can be set to `FALSE` for ignoring such errors, but it is as of no use here. I am guessing this issue is not strictly about this package but I was hoping for a guidance in the right direction.

title: Transactions fail with Amazon Redshift and RPostgres
BIGINT read/write support
description:
- On read RPostgres BIGINTs silently get truncated to 4 bytes but show up as R double types in the returned data frame. I'm guessing that they get cast as R integers here: 
  https://github.com/rstats-db/RPostgres/blob/7ffe0d6bb3f72939461ba386af114cd9357311d6/src/PqResult.h#L257
  but later recast as double.
- dbWriteTable with COPY _seems_ to use scientific notation when formatting numbers (based on the error below). For some reason this generates an error when inserting a large number into a BIGINT; this doesn't happen if inserting into a numeric type or if COPY is disabled and SQL is generated. 
- Less important, dbWriteTable selects 4 byte REAL type for R double types, which can also cause silent data corruption on write. This should probably be a 8 byte "DOUBLE PRECISION" type.
  https://github.com/rstats-db/RPostgres/blob/eb064d445e5c4b7613e5c9d062676b545f737306/R/connection.R#L106

```
library(DBI)
library(RPostgres)

show_table = function(conn, table = "test_bigints") {
  dbGetQuery(conn, 
             sprintf("select column_name, data_type as field_type, character_maximum_length
                from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS where table_name = %s;", dbQuoteString(conn, table)))
}

conn <- dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres())
x <- data.frame(db_variables = c(127, 32767, 8388607, 2147483647, 4294967295))

# Basic case
# RPostgres::dbWriteTable selects REAL (4 bytes) when creating a table. 
# This corrupts silently on insert.
# Same effect if we disable COPY
dbWriteTable(conn, "test_bigints", x, temporary = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE, copy = TRUE)
y = dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT db_variables FROM test_bigints")
show_table(conn)
cbind(x$db_variables, typeof(x$db_variables), y, (y == x$db_variables))

# What if we create our own table with a correct type?
# Seems to work, but looks like we have a problem getting them back
dbExecute(conn, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS test_bigints ")
dbExecute(conn, "CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE test_bigints (db_variables INT8)")
dbWriteTable(conn, "test_bigints", x, temporary = TRUE, append = TRUE, copy = TRUE)
y = dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT db_variables FROM test_bigints")
show_table(conn)
cbind(x$db_variables, typeof(x$db_variables), y, (y == x$db_variables))

# Looks like BIGINTs are getting cast wrong, works fine if we 
# pull them down as numeric
y = dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT db_variables::numeric FROM test_bigints")
show_table(conn)
cbind(x$db_variables, typeof(x$db_variables), y, (y == x$db_variables))

# What if we go bigger, to a true BIGINT? We throw an error for invalid syntax!
local_variables_2 = c(x$db_variables, 1051583408235890)
x2 <- data.frame(db_variables = local_variables_2)
dbWriteTable(conn, "test_bigints", x2, temporary = TRUE, append = TRUE, copy = TRUE)

#Error in eval(substitute(expr), envir, enclos) : 
#  ERROR:  invalid input syntax for integer: "1.05158340823589e+15"
#CONTEXT:  COPY test_bigints, line 6, column db_variables: "1.05158340823589e+15"

# But not if we use SQL statements rather than a COPY stream
dbExecute(conn, "TRUNCATE TABLE test_bigints")
dbWriteTable(conn, "test_bigints", x2, temporary = TRUE, append = TRUE, copy = FALSE)
y = dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT db_variables::numeric FROM test_bigints")
show_table(conn)
cbind(local_variables_2, y, y == local_variables_2)

# Oddly enough we can write with COPY into a DOUBLE PRECISION data type
dbExecute(conn, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS test_bigints ")
dbExecute(conn, "CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE test_bigints (db_variables DOUBLE PRECISION)")
dbWriteTable(conn, "test_bigints", x2, temporary = TRUE, append = TRUE, copy = TRUE)
y = dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT db_variables::numeric FROM test_bigints")
show_table(conn)
cbind(local_variables_2, y, y == local_variables_2)

dbDisconnect(conn)


```

``` r
  RPostgres::Postgres(),
  host = 'localhost',
  port = 5432,
```

title: POSIX binding drops TZ
description:
The TZ is preserved with `dbWriteTable` but not with a query.

```r
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), host="...", user="...", password="...")
dbExecute(con, "drop table if exists quux")
# [1] 0
dbExecute(con, "create table quux (id INT, dt TIMESTAMPTZ)")
# [1] 0
( now <- Sys.time() )
# [1] "2018-07-24 21:55:11 PDT"
dbExecute(con, sprintf("insert into quux (id,dt) values (1,'%s')",
                       withr::with_options(list(digits.secs=6), format(now, usetz=TRUE))))
# [1] 1
res <- dbSendStatement(con, "insert into quux (id,dt) values ($1,$2)")
dbBind(res, list(2L, now))
dbGetRowsAffected(res)
# [1] 1
dbClearResult(res)
dbWriteTable(con, "quux", data.frame(id=3L, dt=now), append=TRUE)
dbGetQuery(con, "select * from quux")
#   id                  dt
# 1  1 2018-07-24 21:55:11
# 2  2 2018-07-24 14:55:11
# 3  3 2018-07-24 21:55:11
dbGetQuery(con, "select cast(dt as varchar(32)) as dtchr from quux")
#                           dtchr
# 1 2018-07-25 04:55:11.522752+00
# 2        2018-07-24 21:55:11+00
# 3 2018-07-25 04:55:11.522752+00
```

(I'm currently in `PDT` aka `-07`.) The first (direct, no binding) and third (`dbInsertTable`) seem to work, but the parameter is [being converted with `as.character`](https://github.com/r-dbi/RPostgres/blob/e85e9399ce2463d162f6366304c24dcc03b1a824/R/PqResult.R#L211) instead of perhaps `format_keep_na`.

In this instance, win10, R-3.3, RPostgres-1.1.1, DBI-1.0.0. I'll test in R-3.4 eventually, but I thought the use of `as.character` to be version-ambivalent.

title: Request to have "dbUpsertTable"
description:
It'd be nice to have a function that performed upserts on multiple rows of a database table in the spirit of dbWriteTable. This functionality was introduced in Postgres 9.5. 

At the moment I've come up with an R written wrapper to perform such upserts in a single row but the performance is much too slow, specially when iterating through many rows.

```
upsert.wrapper <- function(con.x, target_table, 
    unique_constraints, update_vars, new_values){
    names.aux <- names(new_values)
    new_values <- as.character(new_values)
    new_values[new_values == "NA"] <- NA

    q.string <- paste0(
        "INSERT INTO ", target_table, 
        "(", paste0(names.aux, collapse = ","),") VALUES (", 
        new_values %>% 
            dbQuoteString(DBI::ANSI(), .) %>%
            paste0(collapse = ", "), 
        ") ON CONFLICT (", paste(unique_constraints, collapse = ", "),")
        DO UPDATE SET ",
        paste0(update_vars, " = ", "EXCLUDED.", update_vars, collapse = ", ")
    )

    db.q <- dbSendQuery(con.x, q.string)
    out <- dbGetRowsAffected(db.q)
    invisible(dbClearResult(db.q))
}
```

I wonder if there are plans to add this functionality using lower level C++ code, as I suspect this would enhance performance a lot. 

I'd be happy to contribute to this end if you think it's viable. If you do I'd greatly appreciate some pointers on how to get started on this.

title: A Postgres data source for dbplyr?
description:
`PqConnection` currently works with `dbplyr`, but only using the [default translation](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/master/R/translate-sql-base.r). It works for most commonly-used functions, but fails when Postgres has slightly different functions.

For instance, `na_if()` is translated to `NULL_IF()` [in dbplyr](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/master/R/translate-sql-base.r#L132) by default. Postgres has the function `NULLIF()` ([link](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.3/static/functions-conditional.html#FUNCTIONS-NULLIF)) instead.

Other database packages include a file that creates a data source for dbplyr and includes database-specific translations (like [this one](https://github.com/r-dbi/bigrquery/blob/master/R/dplyr.R) for BigQuery). Should we have one for RPostgres too?

title: dbi translation to SQL code skips postgres translations
description:
I gathered the following code from:  https://apps.fishandwhistle.net/archives/1503

```
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)

translate_sql_(
  list(call("%in%", quote(arg1), quote(arg2))),
  con = simulate_dbi()
)
test_call <- function(fun_name, n_args = 1) {
  args <- map(seq_len(n_args), ~ sym(paste0("arg", .x))) %>%
    map(enquote)
  do.call(call, c(list(fun_name), args))
}

test_translate <- function(call, con = simulate_dbi()) {
  translate_sql_(
    list(call),
    con = con
  )
}

sql_variants <- tibble(
  variant = getNamespace("dbplyr") %>%
    names() %>%
    str_subset("^simulate_") %>%
    str_remove("^simulate_"),
  test_connection = map(
    variant,
    ~ getNamespace("dbplyr")[[paste0("simulate_", .x)]]()
  ),
  fun_name = map(test_connection, ~ unique(names(sql_translate_env(.x)))),
)
translations <- crossing(
  tibble(
    n_args = c(0:3, 50)
  ),
  sql_variants
) %>%
  unnest(fun_name, .drop = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(
    call = map2(fun_name, n_args, test_call),
    translation = map2(
      call, test_connection,
      quietly(safely(test_translate))
    ),
    r = map_chr(call, ~ paste(format(.x), collapse = "")),
    sql = map_chr(translation, ~ first(as.character(.x$result$result))),
    messages = map_chr(translation, ~ paste(.x$messages, collapse = "; ") %>% na_if("")),
    warnings = map_chr(translation, ~ paste(.x$warnings, collapse = "; ") %>% na_if("")),
    errors = map_chr(translation, ~ first(as.character(.x$result$error)))
  )

translations %>%
  filter(!is.na(sql), n_args == 1) %>%
  select(variant, n_args, r, sql)
```
This snippet shows that `postgres` is treated differently from the other back ends:
```
translations %>%
  filter(!is.na(sql)) %>% count(variant)
```

``` r
             dplyr::select(mtcars, -hp))
```
I have digged down to the code of the method `dbWriteTable()` and I suspect that the problem may be in `sqlData()`, which [is used inside `dbWriteTable()` ](https://github.com/r-dbi/RPostgres/blob/fc93f1c9567e583a8d0f40844c1f7f847ae51fc4/R/tables.R#L111) after the table [has been created with the appropriate data types](https://github.com/r-dbi/RPostgres/blob/fc93f1c9567e583a8d0f40844c1f7f847ae51fc4/R/tables.R#L102) (i.e. specifying those columns as integers).

This is what I get when I apply `sqlData()` to `mtcars`. Please note the data type and the third element in the column `hp`.
``` r
str(sqlData(con, mtcars))
#> 'data.frame':    32 obs. of  11 variables:
```

However, this doesn't happen when I provide another connection type as first argument to `sqlData()` (for example, an SQL Server connection through odbc).

``` r
str(sqlData(odbc_con, mtcars))
```

title: Fails to compile in CentOS7 (fails to find existing libpq-fe.h)
description:
I try to compile "rstats-db/RPostgres", but it fails to find libpq-fe.h:

```
> devtools::install_github("rstats-db/RPostgres")
Downloading github repo rstats-db/RPostgres@master
Installing RPostgres
'/usr/lib64/R/bin/R' --vanilla CMD INSTALL  \
  '/tmp/Rtmpyy794p/devtoolsc997c6bf0ba/rstats-db-RPostgres-1f09a16'  \
  --library='/home/esa/R/x86_64-redhat-linux-gnu-library/3.1' --install-tests 

* installing *source* package ‘RPostgres’ ...
File libpq-fe.h not found. Please install libpq, e.g: postgresql-devel (rpm) or libpq-dev (deb)
ERROR: configuration failed for package ‘RPostgres’
* removing ‘/home/esa/R/x86_64-redhat-linux-gnu-library/3.1/RPostgres’
Error: Command failed (1)
```

In CentOS7, in order to get Postgresql 9.3 I use pgdg repo, and devel package includes are not in a standard place:

```
[root@localhost bin]# rpm -qil postgresql93-devel | grep libpq-fe
/usr/pgsql-9.3/include/libpq-fe.h
```

And that is also, what is reported by pg_config:

```
[root@localhost bin]# pg_config
BINDIR = /usr/pgsql-9.3/bin
DOCDIR = /usr/share/doc/pgsql
HTMLDIR = /usr/share/doc/pgsql
INCLUDEDIR = /usr/pgsql-9.3/include
[...]
```

title: Truncated digits
error: ‘mem_fn’ is not a member of ‘std’ when building on Travis
description:
I seem to be having this issue on Travis xenial with oldrel R (example: https://travis-ci.org/jonkeane/dbtest/jobs/620860359#L899), I'm not sure why it's not happening elsewhere.

I suspect that this is a similar issue to https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/issues/304 since https://github.com/r-dbi/RPostgres/blob/master/src/DbDataFrame.cpp#L52 is very similar to before the change that was made at https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/compare/r-2.1.3...r-2.1.4#diff-f830d6d7109dc69475f8059eddbf2d6bL52-R52.
